title: The Alpaca, the Urn, and the Grumpy Olive
markdown:
On a peculiar Tuesday in the Museum of Peculiar Things, a catastrophe of fluff was narrowly, and rather funnily, averted.

In halls where behemoth bones loomed and ancient armour stood sentinel, Alistair Fluffernutter presided as station master. He was an alpaca of prodigious fluff and more prodigious self-importance. His wool, pristine cream, was forever immaculately groomed. Each step was a measured ballet. He believed himself the embodiment of station-masterly refinement, a pillar of decorum in a world that had misplaced its manners. His serious expression, usually as unyielding as well-set pottery, was his most treasured possession.

The Tuesday had already cracked that composure. Pre-breakfast exuberance had led him to polish his gleaming brass bell with a touch too much vigour. He nudged a teetering display of ancient Roman pottery. A significant shard, depicting a rather grumpy olive, tumbled and lodged itself inside a magnificent, slightly dusty Grecian urn.

“Oh, bother and all that,” he muttered. His fluffy ears twitched. The urn was slated for a special viewing that afternoon, an event he had overseen with painstaking care. If the shard were discovered, the ruin would not be pottery. It would be him.

He needed a plan: swift, silent, dignified. He scurried to his office, a haven of lavender and old paper where he usually felt most in control. Today even the parchment smell could not soothe him. He summoned Rosa Quicktail, a weasel of remarkable intelligence whose tail seemed to possess a mind of its own—usually a source of amusement, now a beacon of hope.

“Rosa. A delicate situation. Discretion. Finesse.”

Rosa was sorting lost buttons, each a miniature mystery. She tilted her head. “Finesse? Last time you needed finesse, you ironed your waistcoat while wearing it. The scorch marks.”

He waved a dismissive hoof. “Minor technicality. I may have misplaced a small historical artefact. Inside another artefact. An unfortunate, entirely accidental insertion.”

Her eyes twinkled. “The artefact-in-artefact manoeuvre. A classic. Urgency?”

“Lunchtime. Before the patrons. They must not witness this slight imperfection.” He consulted his pocket watch. “Two hours. The consequences for my reputation—”

They could not risk disturbing the urn further; the clay might crumble. Alistair declared, with a flourish that would have done a stage magician proud, that the solution was a sign. A clever, discreet sign. A cordon of polite avoidance. Rosa suggested they simply explain. He overruled her with shaky decisiveness.

“Subtlety is key.”

Velvet ropes, rich crimson against the museum’s muted tones. A large, hastily painted board. He insisted on the finest calligraphy pens, each stroke a testament to appearances. Rosa painted, sighing in the particular way reserved for Alistair’s grand phrasing.

The sign, bold and slightly wobbly, read:

ATTENTION DISCERNING VISITORS: THIS IMPRESSIVE VESSEL IS TEMPORARILY OUT OF ORDER. PLEASE ADMIRE ITS EXTERNAL GRANDEUR ONLY.

“Perfect. Discreet. Dignified. A masterpiece of subtle suggestion.”

The visitors arrived, footsteps soft on polished floors. The sign, written by an alpaca in a panic and read by an eager public, did not discourage. It attracted.

“Out of order?” whispered Mrs Higgins, whose collection of antique thimbles was rivalled only by her capacity for gossip. “How peculiar. What’s wrong with it. Haunted, do you think?”

Young Timmy, prodigious of imagination and fond of poking, peered until his nose nearly touched the rope. “Maybe it’s got a ghost inside,” he stage-whispered. His mother, to Alistair’s horror, nodded thoughtfully.

A small crowd gathered, then a larger one, as crowds will when a sign forbids them the one thing they now most want. They were not admiring external grandeur. They were speculating about internal woes: hidden treasures, secret passages, a mechanism left running since Rome, spectral inhabitants with opinions about olives. A scholar asked whether Out of Order was a newly discovered school of urn. From his office window Alistair felt his wool prickle with cold dread. This was not a dignified diversion. This was a hive of imagination, all focused on the very thing he wished to hide.

Then a rather enthusiastic gentleman, convinced the urn hid a secret mechanism or a stubborn dust bunny, gave it a robust tap with his walking stick. Not a dull thud: a faint hollow clink that seemed to travel the floorboards. Old dust. Anxious alpaca. The olive shard shifted on its perch.

Alistair gasped. He could see it now: a pale sliver of pottery, the grumpy olive’s eye, peeking from the urn’s mouth. He imagined headlines. His carefully constructed world of perfection was about to shatter—and, worse, the museum with it.

He could not bear the thought of the sanctuary damaged, or of visitors who had come for knowledge going home with a cracked story. The flaw was not only his. It might become theirs.

With a heaving sigh that rustled his impeccable wool, Alistair Fluffernutter left the office. He walked, not with measured dignity but with a determined wobbly gait, straight to the crowd. The lavender of his desk felt miles away. A hundred gazes waited.

“Esteemed patrons. I must confess. The sign was my doing. A discreet solution that was not. And the urn—” He paused. His fluffy knees felt suddenly weak. “The urn did not start this way.”

He explained the bell, polished with too much morning pride; the nudge; the rather grumpy olive that had chosen the urn as a hiding place. He spoke of his need to look flawless, of the two hours he had spent on ropes and calligraphy instead of tweezers, and how hiding a small embarrassment had made a larger one, complete with rumours of ghosts. The crowd listened without the judgment he had rehearsed for headlines. Mrs Higgins tutted, mild and almost kind, as if antique thimbles had taught her that small objects wander. Timmy looked briefly disappointed about the ghost, then intrigued by a very real olive with a face.

Rosa hopped onto a nearby pedestal. “Don’t fret. We can fix this. Teamwork, and a very long pair of tweezers.”

She produced the tweezers from her satchel—the same tool she used for delicate button retrieval. “If you could hold that urn ever so still, sir,” she said to the gentleman with the stick, who, eager to be useful, obliged.

Rosa leaned until her whiskers nearly entered history. A delicate scrape. A faint rattle as the shard nudged clay. The gentleman held his breath as if breath itself might topple Greece. Then, with a triumphant flick of her wrist, out came the errant olive, its grumpy expression intact, a little dustier, no wiser.

A collective sigh swept the hall. The urn, though it would always remember a foolish alpaca and an olive, was whole. No ghost. No secret passage. Only a shard that had wanted, briefly, to be important.

Alistair’s smile, for once unpracticed, reached his eyes. “Recovered. With friends who are excellent at errant pottery.”

The hall applauded, warm. He felt at ease; his wool no longer prickled. The museum, and Rosa, mattered more than a perfect face.

As for the shard? He commissioned a tiny velvet-lined case, a miniature throne. The label, in a hand now less wobbly, read: The Grumpy Olive of Alexandria. A reminder that tweezers, and telling the truth, sort even the sulkiest fruit.

The afternoon viewing went ahead, a little late and a great deal more honest. Visitors admired the urn’s external grandeur after all—and then, smiling, queued for the olive on its little throne. Children pressed their noses to the glass. Mrs Higgins declared it a finer gossip than a haunting. Timmy waved at the grumpy face as if they were now colleagues. Alistair stood nearby without a sign, without a rope, and found that the hall did not fall down when he failed to look perfect. The olive, no longer a secret, was somehow more itself.
audience: children aged 11-12, amusing story for older children
